Price basis
Total-return index: dividends are reinvested. This is the default; switch to Price Return to leave dividends out.

GPIndexed performance (NAV, rebased to 100)

How to read this

Each index's total-return level is rebased to 100 at the start of the window, so every path starts from the same footing and can be compared like for like.

The source is the NSE total-return index level, with dividends reinvested. The plotted series is level / level[start] × 100. The Log toggle puts the y-axis on a log scale, so equal percentage moves look equal in size. Drag the range slider or box-zoom to focus on any sub-window; hovering shows every series at that date.

This is the first read on any desk: who compounded more, and how the lead built up over time.

COMPComparative statistics

How to read this

The standard return and risk scorecard over the chosen window, one row per series, with a CAGR and alpha bar chart beneath it.

Every figure uses the active window and frequency. Total is level[end]/level[start]−1. CAGR is (level[end]/level[start])365/days−1, counted in calendar days. Vol is volatility, stdev(returns)·√ppy. Sharpe is (mean−rf)·ppy ÷ vol. Sortino is the same idea, but only downside deviation goes in the denominator. MaxDD is the maximum drawdown, min(level/cummax−1). Calmar is CAGR ÷ |MaxDD|. Best/Worst 1Y are the highest and lowest trailing one-year returns. α is CAGR(series) − CAGR(primary benchmark). Here ppy means periods per year: 252 for daily data, 52 for weekly.

CAGR alone is a trap. Read return, risk and drawdown together.

αRolling alpha & beta vs benchmark

How to read this

Rolling α (Excess) is the trailing-window return of the index minus the benchmark's, annualized when the window is a year or longer and cumulative when it is shorter. Rolling α (Jensen) is the intercept of r_index − rf = α + β·(r_bench − rf) fitted over the trailing window, annualized. It is the part of the return that market exposure does not explain.

Rolling β is cov(r_index, r_bench) / var(r_bench) over the trailing window: how sensitive the index is to the benchmark.

A single full-period alpha hides when the edge actually showed up. The rolling view shows which regimes it depended on.

RISKRolling risk

How to read this

Drawdown is level/running-max − 1, the underwater curve. Volatility is the rolling stdev(returns)·√ppy. Sharpe is the rolling (mean−rf)·ppy ÷ volatility. Correlation is the rolling correlation between the index and the benchmark. Relative strength is the index price divided by the benchmark price, rebased to 100.

Investor experience lives here: how deep and how long the pain, how bumpy the ride, and how closely the pair moves together.

CORRCorrelation matrix

How to read this

The full pairwise correlation of all selected series, indices and benchmarks alike, with each other, over the chosen window and frequency. It is not just each series against the benchmark.

Each cell is the Pearson correlation of the daily returns of that pair, computed on the dates both series have in common. The colour scale is continuous: green is high (+1), yellow is the middle (0), red is low (−1). The deeper the green, the higher the correlation.

It shows which holdings actually diversify each other and which move together. The rolling line above only compares each index to the benchmark.

CAPUp / down capture

How to read this

How much of the benchmark's up-moves and down-moves each index captures. Up is Σ(index ret | bench>0) ÷ Σ(bench ret | bench>0). Down is Σ(index ret | bench<0) ÷ Σ(bench ret | bench<0). Ratio is Up ÷ Down.

A good profile captures the upside (a high Up) while ducking the downside (a low Down, so a Ratio well above 1). In the scatter, points below the 45° line are the favourable ones.

CYCalendar-year returns & alpha

How to read this

Total return for each calendar year: year-end level ÷ prior year-end level − 1. The first year uses the window start as its base and is marked *. Alpha is the year's return minus the primary benchmark's return for the same year.

The % positive and % negative under each chart count the calendar years in which that series was up or down. For the alpha chart they count the years with alpha above or below zero.

This shows consistency, and which years helped or hurt, without any rolling-window smoothing.

Calendar-year total return
Calendar-year alpha vs primary benchmark
* = partial first year (window start ≠ Jan 1)

SEASMonthly-return heatmap

How to read this

A month-by-year grid of monthly total returns (month-end ÷ prior month-end − 1) for the selected index. Green is a positive month, red a negative one.

It brings out seasonality and shows which months drove or dragged a year.

DISTReturn & alpha distributions

How to read this

The distribution of rolling, overlapping returns at four horizons: monthly, quarterly, yearly and three-year. The three-year figure is a CAGR; the others are cumulative. Each is drawn as a smooth density curve (a Gaussian kernel density) rather than bars, so several indices can be overlaid cleanly. Below them are the same four horizons for alpha against the primary benchmark.

At each date the trailing return for that horizon is computed (the trailing one-year return, for example), and the curve is the smoothed frequency distribution of those overlapping observations. A horizon longer than the selected window is left out, and only that one chart is affected. The y-axis is probability density, so the area under each curve is 1.

It shows the full shape of outcomes at each horizon, the centre, the spread, the skew and the tails, not just one average.

Valuation metric

VALValuation over time

How to read this

The actual valuation level of each selected index over the window: P/E, P/B or dividend yield. It is not rebased; the number itself is the information.

The source is NSE's published daily index P/E, P/B and dividend-yield series. P/E is index price ÷ trailing earnings; P/B is price ÷ book value; dividend yield is trailing dividend ÷ price, in %. The dashed band around each series is its window mean ±1σ (the lighter band) and ±2σ, the range the series tends to revert towards.

This is the first valuation read: is the index trading rich or cheap against where it usually sits, and is it stretching away from its band?

RICH / CHEAPWhere each index sits in its own history

How to read this

The cheap/rich gauge: for each index, where today's valuation sits within its own history over the window.

The percentile is the share of the window's observations at or below the current value, so 80% means the index is dearer than it has been 80% of the time. The z-score is (current − window mean) ÷ window σ. For P/E and P/B a high percentile means expensive (rich); for dividend yield it is the other way round, since a high yield means cheap. The pin marks the current percentile on the green-to-red scale.

"Is 22× expensive?" only means something against that index's own range. This answers it at a glance, in a way that is comparable across indices.

CROSS-SECTIONSnapshot — who is cheapest now

How to read this

The current valuation of every selected series side by side, ranked, each with its own-history percentile.

The bars show the latest value of each series, most expensive first; for dividend yield the highest yield, which is the cheapest, comes first. The label carries the own-history percentile and the rich/cheap tag.

It is the relative-value read across the watchlist in one frame: which index is the dear one and which is the bargain right now.

SPREADValuation spread vs primary benchmark

How to read this

Each index's valuation minus the primary benchmark's, over time, for example Midcap P/E − NIFTY 500 P/E. It shows relative richness.

The spread is index value − primary-benchmark value on each date the two share. The line beneath the chart reports the latest spread, its window mean, and its percentile within the window.

Absolute valuation drifts with the whole market. The spread isolates whether a segment is getting expensive relative to the broad market, which is a classic mean-reversion read.

DISTValuation distribution

How to read this

The distribution of each index's valuation over the window, drawn as a smooth density with the current value marked. It is the full shape of where the index has traded.

The curve is a Gaussian kernel density of the window's daily values. A current value out to the right sits in the expensive tail; for a yield it sits in the cheap tail.

It shows whether today is a normal level or an outlier, and how wide the index's valuation range has been.

Company
A per-stock quant and market-intelligence cockpit: market behaviour, business and valuation checks, ownership and governance, and a transparent rule-based research snapshot. Diagnostics only, not buy or sell advice.
Earnings Revision A screen across the NSE 500 for stocks that are already in a price correction and whose fundamentals are deteriorating. They are split into four quadrants by two questions: are sell-side analysts turning positive (LSEG StarMine ARM, the analyst revisions model), and are fund managers net buyers (our corporate-action-adjusted active flow)? Diagnostics only, not buy or sell advice.
Scheme
A look through a mutual fund's portfolio: asset and sector mix, top holdings and concentration, taken from the AMC's monthly SEBI portfolio disclosure. Diagnostics only.
Scheme
Fund-manager skill measured from holdings: excess return against the SEBI category benchmark, its statistical significance (t = IR·√years, where IR is the information ratio), stock-selection skill (IC, the information coefficient), sizing and concentration. Everything is computed from 13 years of monthly portfolios on a total-return basis, gross of costs and before any factor deflation. Diagnostics only, not advice.
Macro & cross-asset Global rates, the rupee and the dollar, commodities, volatility, credit and crypto, over the window set here. The India series (CPI, the repo rate, the India 10-year yield, foreign and domestic institutional flows) come first.
Events & corporate actions The corporate tape, straight from the exchange: who reports when (results calendar and board meetings), which ex-dates are coming (dividends, splits, bonuses), who traded size (bulk, block and short deals), who is building or selling a stake (SAST takeover disclosures), what is listing (IPOs) and what companies have just told the exchange (announcements). Text and tables only; every table sorts on click and exports to CSV. This is a disclosure record, not buy or sell advice.
Earnings Revisions Sell-side earnings-estimate revisions from LSEG StarMine ARM, screened into a quarterly rebalance shortlist. Every ranked list is limited to names that are fresh, tradable and resolved to a symbol (the in_universe flag); a stale or untradable name is dropped, never smoothed over. Lists are ranked by the level of the score, not by its recent change. Diagnostics only, not buy or sell advice.
Gold Gold pays no cash flow, so its price moves inversely to confidence in cash flows priced in paper money. Every spread here (the India premium, the sovereign gold bond discount, the Shanghai premium, the futures carry) is computed by us from primary quotes, never taken from commentary. Each panel carries its own content date. A source that is not wired up yet says pending source and why, instead of showing an empty chart. These are inputs for judgement, not buy or sell advice.
Power India's electricity system in numbers: energy met and peak shortage (from the CEA/NPP daily generation report), generation by fuel and the renewable share, coal stock at plants in days of burn, and installed capacity. Every series names its source and formula. A feed that has not landed says so instead of showing an empty chart.
Consumption What the economy actually burns and buys, in physical units: petroleum products by type from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC). Diesel stands for freight and farms, petrol for the vehicle fleet, LPG for households and aviation turbine fuel for air travel. More consumption feeds (vehicle sales, air passengers, rail freight, digital payments) will join as their sources are proven.
Oil Oil is a flow commodity balanced by inventories, and the futures curve is the market's own daily inventory report. Backwardation (near-dated barrels priced above later ones) says barrels are wanted now; contango beyond the cost of storage says glut. Crack spreads, the gap between refined product prices and crude, show whether the world is short of crude or short of refined product. The India panel turns all of it into what the economy actually pays. Every proxy is labelled, and a source that is not wired up yet says pending source and why. These are inputs for judgement, not buy or sell advice.
